The '''68th Academy Awards''' ceremony, organized by the [[Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences]] (AMPAS), honored the best [[1995 in film|films of 1995]] in the United States and took place on March 25, 1996, at the [[Dorothy Chandler Pavilion]] in Los Angeles beginning at 6:00&nbsp;p.m. [[Pacific Time Zone|PST]] / 9:00&nbsp;p.m. [[Eastern Time Zone|EST]].<ref name=VarietyOscars>{{cite news|last=Lowry |first=Brian |title=Review: "The 68th Annual Academy Awards" |url=https://variety.com/1996/tv/reviews/the-68th-annual-academy-awards-1200445226/ |access-date=August 26, 2013 |work=[[Variety (magazine)|Variety]] |publisher=[[Penske Media Corporation]] |date=March 26, 1996 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131023144229/http://variety.com/1996/tv/reviews/the-68th-annual-academy-awards-1200445226/ |archive-date=October 23, 2013 }}</ref> During the ceremony, AMPAS presented [[Academy Awards]] (commonly referred to as Oscars) in 24 categories.<ref name=VarietyOscars/> The ceremony, televised in the United States by [[American Broadcasting Company|ABC]], was produced by [[David Salzman]] and [[Quincy Jones]] and directed by [[Jeff Margolis]].<ref name=VarietyOscars/> Actress [[Whoopi Goldberg]] hosted the show for the second time, having previously presided over the [[66th Academy Awards|66th ceremony]] in 1994.<ref>{{cite news|title=Whoopi Goldberg To Be Oscars Host |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1995/11/01/movies/whoopi-goldberg-to-be-oscars-host.html |access-date=October 1, 2013 |work=The New York Times |date=November 1, 1995 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131004214534/http://www.nytimes.com/1995/11/01/movies/whoopi-goldberg-to-be-oscars-host.html |archive-date=October 4, 2013 }}</ref> Three weeks earlier, in a ceremony held at the [[Beverly Wilshire Hotel|Regent Beverly Wilshire Hotel]] in [[Beverly Hills, California]], on March 2, the [[Academy Award for Technical Achievement|Academy Awards for Technical Achievement]] were presented by host [[Richard Dreyfuss]].<ref>{{cite news|title=Past Scientific & Technical Awards Ceremonies|url=http://www.oscars.org/awards/scitech/pastawards.html|access-date=July 31, 2013|work=[[Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences]]|publisher=AMPAS|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140213185729/http://www.oscars.org/awards/scitech/pastawards.html|archive-date=February 13, 2014}}</ref>

''[[Braveheart]]'' won five awards, including [[Academy Award for Best Picture|Best Picture]].<ref>{{cite news|last=Welkos |first=Robert W. |title='Braveheart' Is Top Film; Cage, Sarandon Win |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1996-03-26-mn-51422-story.html |access-date=October 2, 2013 |work=Los Angeles Times |date=March 26, 1996 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120309193628/http://articles.latimes.com/1996-03-26/news/mn-51422_1_sarandon-win |archive-date=March 9, 2012 }}</ref><ref>{{cite news|last=Hartl |first=John |title=One More Victory For 'Braveheart' – Mel Gibson's Epic About A Battle For Freedom Tops The Oscars |url=https://archive.seattletimes.com/archive/19960326/2321029/one-more-victory-for-braveheart----mel-gibsons-epic-about-a-battle-for-freedom-tops-the-oscars |access-date=October 1, 2013 |work=[[The Seattle Times]] |publisher=[[The Seattle Times Company]] |date=March 25, 1996 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131004212951/http://community.seattletimes.nwsource.com/archive/?date=19960326&slug=2321029 |archive-date=October 4, 2013 }}</ref> Other winners included ''[[Apollo 13 (film)|Apollo 13]]'', ''[[Pocahontas (1995 film)|Pocahontas]]'', ''[[Restoration (1995 film)|Restoration]]'', and ''[[The Usual Suspects]]'' with two awards and ''[[Anne Frank Remembered]]'', ''[[Antonia's Line]]'', ''[[Babe (film)|Babe]]'', ''[[A Close Shave]]'', ''[[Dead Man Walking (film)|Dead Man Walking]]'', ''[[Leaving Las Vegas]]'', ''[[Lieberman in Love]]'', ''[[Mighty Aphrodite]]'', ''[[One Survivor Remembers]]'', ''[[Il Postino: The Postman]]'', and ''[[Sense and Sensibility (1995 film)|Sense and Sensibility]]'' with one. The telecast garnered almost 45 million viewers in the United States.

==Winners and nominees==
<!-- Please do not add any fact or statement below unless you have a credible source verifying it. Otherwise, it will be promptly removed. -->

The nominees for the 68th Academy Awards were announced on February 13, 1996, at 5:38&nbsp;a.m. [[Pacific Time Zone|PST]] (13:38 [[Coordinated Universal Time|UTC]]) at the [[Samuel Goldwyn Theater]] by [[Arthur Hiller]], the president of the academy, and the music producer [[Quincy Jones]].<ref>{{cite news|last=Hicks |first=Chris |title='96 Oscar Nominations are Filled with Surprises |url=https://www.deseret.com/1996/2/13/19224737/96-oscar-nominations-are-filled-with-surprises/ |access-date=May 19, 2026 |work=[[Deseret News]] |date=February 13, 1996 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260519204912/https://www.deseret.com/1996/2/13/19224737/96-oscar-nominations-are-filled-with-surprises/ |archive-date=May 19, 2026 }}</ref> ''[[Braveheart]]'' led all nominees with ten nominations; ''[[Apollo 13 (film)|Apollo 13]]'' came in second with nine.<ref>{{cite news|last=Welkos |first=Robert W. |title=Gibson's Epic Gets 10, 'Babe' Ties for Third |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1996-02-14-ca-40073-story.html |access-date=October 1, 2013 |work=Los Angeles Times |date=February 14, 1996 |author2=Claudia Puig |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131004215351/http://articles.latimes.com/1996-02-14/entertainment/ca-40073_1_oscar-nomination |archive-date=October 4, 2013 }}</ref><ref>{{cite news|last=Weinraug |first=Bernard |title=Oscar Nominations Are Just One Surprise After Another |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1996/02/14/movies/oscar-nominations-are-just-one-surprise-after-another.html |access-date=October 1, 2013 |work=The New York Times |date=February 14, 1996 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131004214825/http://www.nytimes.com/1996/02/14/movies/oscar-nominations-are-just-one-surprise-after-another.html |archive-date=October 4, 2013 }}</ref>

The winners were announced during the awards ceremony on March 25, 1996.<ref>{{cite news|title=The 1996 Academy Awards: And the Winners are... |url=https://www.chicagotribune.com/1996/03/26/and-the-winners-are-5/ |access-date=October 1, 2013 |work=Chicago Tribune |publisher=Tribune Publishing |date=March 26, 1996 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131004213010/http://articles.chicagotribune.com/1996-03-26/news/9603260051_1_sense-and-sensibility-braveheart-gordon-e-sawyer-award |archive-date=October 4, 2013 }}</ref> ''Braveheart'' was the ninth film to win Best Picture with no acting nominations.<ref>{{cite news|last=Dawes|first=Amy|title='Braveheart' Conquers:Gibson's epic wins Best Picture\Sarandon, Cage take acting honors.|url=http://www.thefreelibrary.com/%27BRAVEHEART%27+CONQUERS%5CGibson%27s+epic+wins+Best+Picture%5CSarandon,+Cage...-a083931988|access-date=October 1, 2013|work=[[Los Angeles Daily News]]|publisher=[[MediaNews Group]]|date=March 26, 1996|archive-date=October 4, 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131004215350/http://www.thefreelibrary.com/%27BRAVEHEART%27+CONQUERS%5CGibson%27s+epic+wins+Best+Picture%5CSarandon,+Cage...-a083931988|url-status=dead}}</ref> With her Best Supporting Actress win for ''[[Mighty Aphrodite]]'', Mira Sorvino became the second consecutive actress to win the aforementioned category for a performance in a film directed by [[Woody Allen]].<ref>{{cite news|last=Boyar |first=Jay |title=Predictions And Personal Favorites Of A Movie Fan |url=https://www.orlandosentinel.com/1996/03/24/predictions-and-personal-favorites-of-a-movie-fan/ |access-date=October 1, 2013 |work=[[Orlando Sentinel]] |publisher=Tribune Publishing |date=March 24, 1996 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131004213905/http://articles.orlandosentinel.com/1996-03-24/entertainment/9603210948_1_personal-favorites-sense-and-sensibility-favorite-movie/2 |archive-date=October 4, 2013 }}</ref> Best Adapted Screenplay winner [[Emma Thompson]] was the first person to win Oscars for both acting and screenwriting. She had previously won Best Actress for her performance in the 1992 film ''[[Howards End (film)|Howards End]]''.<ref>{{cite news|last=Saner |first=Emine |title=Emma Thompson: Top 100 Women |url=https://www.theguardian.com/culture/2011/mar/08/emma-thompson-100-women |access-date=October 2, 2013 |work=The Guardian |date=March 7, 2011 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131004215154/http://www.theguardian.com/culture/2011/mar/08/emma-thompson-100-women |archive-date=October 4, 2013 }}</ref> This was the first year since the [[42nd Academy Awards]]—and last to date—that none of the acting winners appeared in Best Picture nominees.

==Ceremony information==
[[File:Whoopi Goldberg at a NYC No on Proposition 8 Rally.jpg|thumbnail|right|[[Whoopi Goldberg]] hosted the 68th Academy Awards.|alt=Photo of Whoopi Goldberg.]]

As a result of the negative reception of [[David Letterman]]'s stint as host from the [[67th Academy Awards|preceding year's ceremony]], veteran film and television director [[Gil Cates]] declined to helm the upcoming festivities.<ref>{{harvnb|Pond|2005|p=100}}</ref> In November 1995, AMPAS recruited music producer and [[Jean Hersholt Humanitarian Award]] recipient [[Quincy Jones]] as producer of the 1996 ceremony.<ref name="Whoopi">{{cite news|last=Puig |first=Claudia |title=An Oscar Duet for Quincy and Whoopi : Television: The noted composer and arranger will produce the 68th annual Academy Awards show, and the actress-comedian will host for a second time. |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1995-11-01-ca-63723-story.html |access-date=October 1, 2013 |work=[[Los Angeles Times]] |date=November 1, 1995 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131004213608/http://articles.latimes.com/1995-11-01/entertainment/ca-63723_1_68th-annual-academy-awards |archive-date=October 4, 2013 }}</ref> Jones immediately selected actress and comedian [[Whoopi Goldberg]] to host the ceremony.<ref name="Whoopi"/> In an interview with ''[[Los Angeles Times]]'' writer Susan King, Jones explained the decision to hire Goldberg saying, "She has all the qualifications to move on a dime, to carry the elegance and the dignity of the show and is very funny. She understands the street. She has everything."<ref>{{cite news|last=King |first=Susan |title=Quincy Jones: 'Pushing the Envelope' |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1996-03-24-tv-50515-story.html |access-date=October 2, 2013 |work=Los Angeles Times |date=March 24, 1996 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131022224343/http://articles.latimes.com/1996-03-24/news/tv-50515_1_quincy-jones |archive-date=October 22, 2013 }}</ref>

One segment that was staged during the ceremony was an elaborate fashion show showcasing the nominees for [[Academy Award for Best Costume Design|Best Costume Design]].<ref name="Fashion show">{{harvnb|Pond|2005|p=114}}</ref> Produced by fashion photographer [[Matthew Rolston]], the production featured models such as [[Cameron Alborzian]], [[Tyson Beckford]], [[Tyra Banks]], [[Marcus Schenkenberg]] and [[Joel West]] sporting various costumes from the five films nominated in the category.<ref>{{harvnb|Pond|2005|p=122}}</ref> Initially, actor [[Jack Nicholson]] was approached to introduce the segment along with models [[Naomi Campbell]] and [[Claudia Schiffer]]. However, actor [[Pierce Brosnan]] accepted the role of presenter of the segment and award after Nicholson declined those respective duties.<ref name="Fashion show" />

Several other people and elements were also involved with the production of the ceremony. Jeff Margolis served as director for the program.<ref>{{harvnb|Pond|2005|p=106}}</ref> Actress and talk show host [[Oprah Winfrey]] interviewed several nominees and other attendees during a seven-minute red carpet arrival segment shown at the beginning of the telecast.<ref>{{harvnb|Pond|2005|p=121}}</ref> Musician and saxophonist [[Tom Scott (saxophonist)|Tom Scott]] served as musical director for the ceremony.<ref name="Babe-Scott">{{harvnb|Pond|2005|p=118}}</ref> Choreographer [[Jamie King]] supervised the performances of the Best Song nominees and two dance numbers.<ref>{{cite news|last=Kleid |first=Beth |title=Movies |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1996-02-19-ca-37594-story.html |access-date=October 1, 2013 |work=Los Angeles Times |date=February 19, 1996 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131004215354/http://articles.latimes.com/1996-02-19/entertainment/ca-37594_1_director-elia-kazan |archive-date=October 4, 2013 }}</ref> Babe, the pig from the [[Babe (film)|eponymous film]], and [[Miss Piggy]] participated in a comedy sketch during the proceedings.<ref name="Babe-Scott"/> Actor [[Christopher Reeve]], who was paralyzed in a horse riding accident nearly a year earlier, made a surprise appearance on the telecast urging filmmakers to make movies that face the world's most important issues head-on.<ref>{{harvnb|Pond|2005|p=127}}</ref>

===Rainbow Coalition protest===
Several days before the ceremony, activist group [[Rainbow/PUSH|Rainbow Coalition]], led by Reverend [[Jesse Jackson]], planned a protest regarding [[African Americans]] and other [[racial minorities]] in the film industry.<ref name="Protest">{{cite news|last=Braxton |first=Greg |title=Jackson Plans Oscar Protest |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1996-03-17-me-48073-story.html |access-date=October 2, 2013 |work=Los Angeles Times |date=March 17, 1996 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131004220113/http://articles.latimes.com/1996-03-17/local/me-48073_1_jesse-jackson |archive-date=October 4, 2013 }}</ref> The group was voicing its objections to unflattering portrayals of minorities in film and television and the fact that minorities were underemployed in the entertainment industry.<ref name="Protest"/> Jackson further pointed out the disparity in racial minorities in Hollywood by noting that Best Live Action Short Film nominee [[Dianne Houston]] was the only African American nominated that year.<ref>{{cite news|last1=Trescott |first1=Jacqueline |title=You Are Dealing with a Three-Headed Beast |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/lifestyle/style/1996/03/24/you-are-dealing-with-a-three-headed-beast/0f82687a-2cd9-452d-a010-7bce05cc7876/ |access-date=October 2, 2013 |newspaper=The Washington Post |date=March 24, 1996 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161106122929/https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/lifestyle/style/1996/03/24/you-are-dealing-with-a-three-headed-beast/0f82687a-2cd9-452d-a010-7bce05cc7876/ |archive-date=November 6, 2016 }}</ref> Although the group initially planned to demonstrate outside the [[Dorothy Chandler Pavilion]], an agreement between Jackson and producer Jones caused the protest to be moved adjacent to the broadcast facilities of the local [[American Broadcasting Company|ABC]] affiliate [[KABC-TV]].<ref>{{harvnb|Bona|2002|p=38}}</ref> Nevertheless, Jones remarked that the Academy Awards were not the appropriate venue for such protest declaring "Why should the movie business be different from anything else in America? It's a problem that permeates everything in the country. Every facet of America discriminates."<ref>{{cite news|last=Kleid |first=Beth |title=Oscar Watch |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1996-03-25-ca-50951-story.html |access-date=October 2, 2013 |work=Los Angeles Times |date=March 25, 1996 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131005004150/http://articles.latimes.com/1996-03-25/entertainment/ca-50951_1_oscar-show |archive-date=October 5, 2013 }}</ref>

===Division of Best Original Score category===
Beginning with this ceremony, the AMPAS music branch divided the category of [[Academy Award for Best Original Score|Best Original Score]] into two categories: Best Dramatic Score and Best Musical or Comedy Score.<ref>{{harvnb|Levy|2003|p=55}}</ref> This was seen as a response to the dominance of [[Walt Disney Feature Animation]] films in the Original Score and Original Song categories in recent years.<ref>{{harvnb|Pond|2005|p=99}}</ref> Four years later, the two scoring categories were merged back into one category.<ref>{{cite news|last=Burlingame |first=Jon |title=Sweet sounds of success |url=https://variety.com/1999/more/news/sweet-sounds-of-success-1117490434/ |access-date=October 2, 2013 |work=Variety |publisher=Penske Media Corporation |date=January 20, 1999 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130511204133/http://variety.com/1999/more/news/sweet-sounds-of-success-1117490434/ |archive-date=May 11, 2013 }}</ref>

===Christopher Reeve appearance===
At the ceremony, [[Christopher Reeve]] presented a montage of films which tackled social issues. His appearance was a surprise to the majority of those present and occurred less than a year after the horse-riding accident in which he was paralyzed. Reeve's appearance was kept secret in part so that if any physical issue came about, he could drop out quietly. He attended an early morning closed-door rehearsal, during which he vetoed the idea of using [[John Williams (composer)|John William]]s' 1978 [[Music of Superman|Superman Theme]] as entrance music. Reeve, along with Jones, had chosen the film clips used in the montage.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Brew |first1=Simon |title=When Christopher Reeve Surprised The World at The Oscars |url=https://www.denofgeek.com/movies/when-christopher-reeve-surprised-the-world-at-the-oscars/ |website=Den of Geek |date=February 22, 2019 |access-date=20 June 2022 |archive-date=June 20, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220620181057/https://www.denofgeek.com/movies/when-christopher-reeve-surprised-the-world-at-the-oscars/ |url-status=live }}</ref> Reeve received a two-minute standing ovation during his appearance.<ref>{{cite web |title=Christopher Reeve at the Oscars |website=[[YouTube]] |date=July 2009 |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ffSy3-PJ5QI |access-date=June 20, 2022 |archive-date=March 18, 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160318231333/https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ffSy3-PJ5QI |url-status=live }}</ref>

===Box office performance of nominees===
At the time of the nominations announcement on February 13, the combined gross of the five Best Picture nominees at the US box office was $333&nbsp;million, with an average of $66.5&nbsp;million per film.<ref name=BoxOfficeOscars>{{cite news|title=1995 Academy Award Nominations and Winner for Best Picture |url=https://boxofficemojo.com/oscar/chart/?yr=1995&p=.htm |access-date=October 1, 2013 |work=[[Box Office Mojo]] |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131004215913/http://boxofficemojo.com/oscar/chart/?yr=1995&p=.htm |archive-date=October 4, 2013 }}</ref> ''Apollo 13'' was the highest earner among the Best Picture nominees with $172&nbsp;million in domestic box office receipts.<ref name=BoxOfficeOscars/> The film was followed by ''Braveheart'' ($67&nbsp;million), ''Babe'' ($58.2&nbsp;million), ''Sense and Sensibility'' ($24.6&nbsp;million) and finally ''Il Postino: The Postman'' ($10.7&nbsp;million).<ref name=BoxOfficeOscars/>

Of the top 50 grossing movies of the year, 47 nominations went to 14 films on the list. Only ''Toy Story'' (2nd), ''Apollo 13'' (3rd), ''Braveheart'' (23rd), ''Babe'' (29th), ''12 Monkeys'' (31st), ''Casino'' (38th) and ''Mr. Holland's Opus'' (39th) were nominated for directing, acting, screenwriting, or Best Picture.<ref name="boxofficemojooscars">{{cite web|url=https://boxofficemojo.com/yearly/chart/?asof=1996-02-13&view=releasedate&view2=domestic&yr=1995&sort=gross&order=DESC&p=.htm |title=1995 Domestic Grosses |work=Box Office Mojo |access-date=February 26, 2014 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151226075842/http://www.boxofficemojo.com/yearly/chart/?asof=1996-02-13&view=releasedate&view2=domestic&yr=1995&sort=gross&order=DESC&p=.htm |archive-date=December 26, 2015 }}</ref> The other box office hits that earned nominations were ''Batman Forever'' (1st), ''Pocahontas'' (4th), ''Seven'' (9th), ''Crimson Tide'' (10th), ''Waterworld'' (12th), ''The Bridges of Madison County'' (21st), ''The American President'' (27th) and ''Sabrina'' (34th).<ref name="boxofficemojooscars"/>

===Critical reviews===
The show received a positive reception from most media publications. ''[[The New York Times]]'' film critic [[Janet Maslin]] raved, "Mr. Jones pointedly turned this year's ceremony into a showcase for Hollywood's new guard." She also praised host Goldberg's opening monologue, remarking that it "established the sharpness of this year's gag writing."<ref>{{cite news|last=Maslin |first=Janet |title=Television Review: Energy, Gallantry, Graphics And Glamour at the Oscars |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1996/03/27/movies/television-review-energy-gallantry-graphics-and-glamour-at-the-oscars.html |access-date=October 1, 2013 |work=The New York Times |date=March 27, 1996 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131004214717/http://www.nytimes.com/1996/03/27/movies/television-review-energy-gallantry-graphics-and-glamour-at-the-oscars.html |archive-date=October 4, 2013 }}</ref> ''[[People (magazine)|People]]'' columnist Janice Min wrote that "the most egregious crime at the 68th Academy Awards on March 25 was–egad!–the relentless elegance and good taste that deprived viewers of genuine, Grade A snicker fodder.<ref>{{cite news|last=Min |first=Janice |title=An Affair To Remember |url=http://www.people.com/people/archive/article/0,,20103212,00.html |access-date=October 1, 2013 |work=[[People (magazine)|People]] |publisher=[[Time Warner]] |date=April 8, 1996 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131004215611/http://www.people.com/people/archive/article/0%2C%2C20103212%2C00.html |archive-date=October 4, 2013 }}</ref> Television critic [[Howard Rosenberg]] of the ''[[Los Angeles Times]]'' applauded Goldberg's performance, noting that her "confident performance [...] was symbolic of her whopping improvement as host over her showing on the [[66th Academy Awards|1994 Oscars]]."<ref>{{cite news|last=Rosenberg |first=Howard |title=Real Drama? It Didn't Come From Ribbons |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1996-03-26-ca-57051-story.html |access-date=October 1, 2013 |work=Los Angeles Times |date=March 26, 1996 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131005010050/http://articles.latimes.com/1996-03-26/entertainment/ca-57051_1_ribbons |archive-date=October 5, 2013 }}</ref>

Some media outlets were more critical of the show. ''[[Chicago Tribune]]'' television critic Steve Johnson lamented that Goldberg "settled into bland script reading that made one long for David Letterman's cranky unpredictability in the role last year." He also stated that the "Best Costume Design fashion show" was the silliest opening Oscar production number since [[Rob Lowe]] and [[Snow White (Disney character)|Snow White]] [[61st Academy Awards#Opening number|sang "Proud Mary" in 1989]].<ref>{{cite news|last=Johnson |first=Steve |title=Whoopi Rises Above The Bland, But Not For Long |url=https://www.chicagotribune.com/1996/03/26/whoopi-rises-above-the-bland-but-not-for-long/ |access-date=October 2, 2013 |work=Chicago Tribune |publisher=Tribune Publishing |date=March 26, 1996 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131004215600/http://articles.chicagotribune.com/1996-03-26/news/9603260063_1_quincy-jones-moments-christopher-reeve |archive-date=October 4, 2013 }}</ref> [[Ken Tucker]] of ''[[Entertainment Weekly]]'' bemoaned that the dominance of Best Picture winner ''Braveheart'' and the lack of fashion glamour "had the makings of a tiresome evening."<ref>{{cite magazine|url=https://ew.com/article/1996/04/05/oscars-1996-show/ |title=Oscars 1996: The Show |date=April 5, 1996 |first=Ken |last=Tucker |magazine=[[Entertainment Weekly]] |publisher=Time Warner |access-date=October 2, 2013 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131004214313/http://www.ew.com/ew/article/0%2C%2C292003%2C00.html |archive-date=October 4, 2013 }}</ref>

===Ratings and reception===
The American telecast on ABC drew in an average of 44.81 million people over its length, which was a 9% decrease from the [[67th Academy Awards|previous year's ceremony]].<ref name="TV By the Numbers">{{cite web |first=Bill |last=Gorman |title=Academy Awards Averages 41.3 Million Viewers; Most Since 2005 |url=http://tvbythenumbers.com/2010/03/08/academy-awards-averages-41-3-million-viewers-most-since-2005/44217 |work=[[TV by the Numbers]] |publisher=[[Tribune Media]] |date=March 8, 2010 |access-date=March 12, 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100310080531/http://tvbythenumbers.com/2010/03/08/academy-awards-averages-41-3-million-viewers-most-since-2005/44217 |archive-date=March 10, 2010 |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref>{{cite news|last=Johnson |first=Greg |title=Call It the Glamour Bowl |url=https://articles.latimes.com/1999/mar/18/business/fi-18458/2 |access-date=August 26, 2013 |work=Los Angeles Times |date=March 18, 1999 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130928053918/http://articles.latimes.com/1999/mar/18/business/fi-18458/2 |archive-date=September 28, 2013 }}</ref> The show also garnered lower [[Nielsen ratings]] compared to the previous ceremony, with 30.48% of households watching over a 48.88 share.<ref name="TVB Oscars">{{cite news|title=Academy Awards ratings |work=Television Bureau of Advertising |url=http://www.tvb.org/media/file/Academy_Awards.pdf |access-date=June 27, 2013 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130515152338/http://www.tvb.org/media/file/Academy_Awards.pdf |archive-date=May 15, 2013 }}</ref> It also earned a lower 18–49 demographic rating with an 18.76 rating over a 35.27 share among viewers in that demographic.<ref name="TVB Oscars" />

In July 1996, the ceremony presentation received seven nominations at the [[48th Primetime Emmy Awards|48th Primetime Emmys]].<ref>{{cite news|title=Primetime Emmy Award database |url=http://www.emmys.com/shows/68th-annual-academy-awards |access-date=October 1, 2013 |publisher=[[Academy of Television Arts and Sciences]] |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131004221456/http://www.emmys.com/shows/68th-annual-academy-awards |archive-date=October 4, 2013 }}</ref> Two months later, the ceremony won one of those nominations for Greg Brunton's lighting design and direction during the telecast.<ref>{{cite news|title=Who Won What: The Winners of Television's Nighttime Emmy Awards |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1996-09-09-ca-42203-story.html |access-date=October 1, 2013 |work=Los Angeles Times |date=September 9, 1996 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131004214104/http://articles.latimes.com/1996-09-09/entertainment/ca-42203_1_nighttime-emmy-awards/2 |archive-date=October 4, 2013 }}</ref>

=="In Memoriam"==
The annual "In Memoriam" tribute was presented by Academy President [[Arthur Hiller]]. The montage featured an excerpt of the main title of ''[[The Prince of Tides]]'' composed by [[James Newton Howard]].<ref>{{harvnb|Bona|2002|p=51}}</ref>

{{div col|colwidth=28em}}
*[[Miklós Rózsa]] – Composer
*[[Ginger Rogers]]
*[[The Andrews Sisters|Maxine Andrews]]
*[[Michael V. Gazzo]]
*[[Dean Martin]]
*[[Viveca Lindfors]]
*[[Martin Balsam]]
*[[Friz Freleng]] – Animator
*[[Burl Ives]]
*[[Butterfly McQueen]]
*[[Dorothy Jeakins]] – Costume Designer
*[[Nancy Kelly]]
*[[Lana Turner]]
*[[Elisha Cook Jr.]]
*[[Ida Lupino]]
*[[Harry Horner]] – Art Director
*[[Terry Southern]] – Writer
*[[Haing S. Ngor]]
*[[Michael Hordern]]
*[[Don Simpson]] – Producer
*[[Ross Hunter]] – Producer
*[[Frank Perry]] – Director
*[[Alexander Godunov]] 
*[[Louis Malle]] – Director
*[[Howard E. Koch|Howard Koch]] – Writer
*[[George Burns]]
{{div col end}}

A separate tribute to actor, dancer and veteran Oscar host [[Gene Kelly]] featured tap dancer [[Savion Glover]] dancing to the song "[[Singin' in the Rain (song)|Singin' in the Rain]]" from the 1952 [[Singin' in the Rain|film of the same name]].<ref>{{cite news|last=Marks |first=Peter |title=On Stage, and Off |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1996/03/22/theater/on-stage-and-off.html |access-date=October 1, 2013 |work=The New York Times |date=March 22, 1996 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150526170608/http://www.nytimes.com/1996/03/22/theater/on-stage-and-off.html |archive-date=May 26, 2015 }}</ref>
